overview: This 448-page State Department file traces narcotics regulation, trafficking, and enforcement involving Japan from 1935 to 1939. Its 281 documents follow trans-Pacific and East Asian networks moving opium, morphine, heroin, and cocaine through Japan, Karafuto, China, Manchukuo, Hawai‘i, Java, and American ports, while recording arrests, seizures, surveillance, shipping controls, addiction treatment, and Japanese laws governing narcotics and cannabis. Diplomatic correspondence also reveals sustained efforts to exchange intelligence with Japanese authorities and the League of Nations, alongside disputes between the State and Treasury Departments over whether American investigators could contact Japanese police directly. Throughout, claims of improved Japanese enforcement coexist uneasily with allegations of official tolerance, corruption, and Japanese-sponsored opium activity in occupied China.
interest: The file is especially valuable for connecting individual smuggling cases to the institutional machinery of international narcotics control: police investigations, customs surveillance, shipping-company searches, diplomatic protocols, and League of Nations reporting. Its unusually detailed records of named suspects, informants, routes, concealment methods, and physical evidence permit close reconstruction of transnational trafficking networks. For historians, the sharp contrast between bilateral cooperation and allegations of Japanese complicity in the drug economy of occupied China illuminates both the practical limits of interwar enforcement and the political uses of narcotics accusations in an age of expanding empire.
